data.content_ref: inline:The target asserts the claim is 'generally false' and that panels 'will not reliably outperform' experts, yet this conclusion depends entirely on the assumed prevalence of tacit-cue-dependent items. The target's own counterconditions concede that if the checklist is complete (condition 4) or if the expert is biased (condition 3), the panel may win. These are not edge cases for tasks with objectively verifiable outcomes—many such tasks (e.g., radiographic fracture detection, loan default prediction) are precisely the domains where actuarial/checklist approaches have empirically matched or beaten expert intuition. The target never establishes that tacit-feature dependence is the modal case rather than the exception, so the strong 'generally false' verdict is unsupported by its own reasoning. A weaker claim ('conditional on tacit-feature prevalence') would be defensible, but the stated conclusion overgeneralizes.
